summary: Research espionage mechanics, intel stats, real 1950s tradecraft, op design, and pillar integration

reports.topic: How strategy games model espionage: what makes it fun vs. a chore, and the core loop shape for 3-6 meaningful espionage decisions per year

findings.name: HoI4 La Résistance: the canonical failure case — churn without payoff
findings.detail: The community verdict is remarkably consistent across the Paradox forums and Steam discussions: (1) The capture-rescue loop is the worst offender — agents get captured semi-randomly, you must stop everything to rescue them, and capture resets network progress, producing 'an annoying circle of pop up messages' that 'feels like a chore' (forum.paradoxplaza.com thread 'Played a few hours of La Resistance', Steam 'La Resistance is Absurdly annoying'). (2) Networks DECAY: 'the network decays so fast that they always get reduced to 0% by the time an operation is finished' — the passive layer actively fights the active layer, so maintaining the precondition for operations is itself micro. (3) Payoffs are opaque and weak: ideology-shift and stability missions 'barely do any damage and can be easily countered', so the dominant strategy is to ignore the whole system ('not really needed if you have a plan') — a dedicated Paradox thread is literally titled 'Spy system too tedious' (forum.paradoxplaza.com/threads/spy-system-too-tedious.1704966). (4) The system is a 'dumbed-down sub-game' disconnected from the main game's stakes. Structural diagnosis: HoI4 made espionage a parallel resource economy (agency upgrades, operative slots, intel network %) with its own maintenance treadmill, whose outputs (a few % intel, minor modifiers) don't feed the decisions the player actually cares about.
findings.recommendation: Never make network upkeep a player job. Networks must not decay from inaction, and agent loss must never generate a mandatory rescue side-quest. Every espionage output must change a decision the player was already making (where deterrence stands, whether reported Soviet steel is real, whether to escalate a crisis) — if an op's payoff is a modifier the player can't feel, cut the op.

findings.name: EU4 spy networks: passive accumulation beats active spending — and that's a design smell worth copying correctly
findings.detail: EU4's model: a diplomat assigned to a country passively builds spy network 0-100; network gives scaling passive bonuses (siege ability, cheaper claims, tech-steal) and can be SPENT on covert actions. Players overwhelmingly found the passive bonuses good and the active actions 'lackluster' — 'more useful having a high network for the bonuses to siege and tech, rather than spending it on an action' (steamcommunity.com/app/236850 discussions; forum thread 'Making espionage & covert actions a smart and worthwhile choice'). The espionage idea group polls near the bottom. But note what DOES work: assigning a diplomat to build a network in the country you intend to invade is a real, legible, one-click strategic commitment with an opportunity cost (that diplomat isn't improving relations elsewhere). The failure was only on the active-spend side: actions were priced so that spending the network you'd built felt like burning your passive bonus for a firecracker. The passive/active split itself is sound — spend-vs-save creates a real decision ONLY if actions are priced to be occasionally irresistible.
findings.recommendation: Adopt EU4's allocation shape — a small number of scarce collection assets pointed at countries, building coverage passively with zero clicks — but invert its pricing failure: active operations must be rare and DECISIVE (reveal the real number behind a rival's reported economy, blow a nuclear program's opacity open), never a trickle of small modifiers, so cashing in coverage is sometimes clearly worth losing it.

findings.name: CK3 schemes: the ramp-and-commit timer works; leverage (hooks) is the best espionage payoff in any strategy game
findings.detail: CK3 schemes build success chance over phases while a secrecy value decays as agents blab; the player choice is WHEN to strike — commit early at low odds or wait and risk exposure (gamewatcher.com, ckstrategyhub.com intrigue guides). That single spend-vs-save timing decision is genuinely good. The community's own verdict is that the best part of intrigue isn't murder but HOOKS: 'the most reliable power in intrigue is not murder but leverage — when you uncover a secret… you can use it as a hook to force cooperation' — a discovered secret becomes a persistent political instrument, not a popup. Criticisms: agent recruitment is fiddly, exposure can silently gut success odds, and 'the AI needs to be able to threaten the player with schemes, or half of the intrigue system is pointless' (forum.paradoxplaza.com thread 'Agents should decrease scheme secrecy'). Two exportable lessons: (a) the payoff that endures — kompromat, a doctored estimate, a mole in place — beats the payoff that resolves; (b) espionage is only tense if the AI is credibly running it against YOU and you can see the shadow of it.
findings.recommendation: Make the flagship covert payoff a HELD INSTRUMENT, not an instant effect: a penetrated ministry that keeps feeding true numbers until burned, kompromat spendable in a crisis ladder for a concession, a mole whose product the player chooses when to act on. And build rival espionage against the player from day one — counterintelligence is only a decision if there's something to counter.

findings.name: Stellaris operations: fire-and-forget with no feedback — the payoff-cadence lesson
findings.detail: Stellaris (Nemesis) assigns an envoy to build infiltration level, then runs multi-phase operations. Community assessment: 'kinda harmless and underwhelming', with the specific diagnosis being NO FEEDBACK — players literally forget they have spy envoys deployed; the 'launch when ready' auto-run tickbox completes operations 'with no notification at all' (forum.paradoxplaza.com 'Espionage - What Good Is It?', steamcommunity.com/app/281990 discussions). Operations are also weak relative to fleet power, so the system is strictly optional. The dual complaint is instructive: the system is SIMULTANEOUSLY a click-fest (each phase step manual) and fire-and-forget (nothing you do matters) — proof that click count and engagement are orthogonal. What players said they wanted is exactly the right spec: 'describe what you want… set priorities, assign resources and wait for results' — intent-level orders, event-level returns.
findings.recommendation: Payoff cadence rule: the player states intent (a standing collection priority, a launched op) in seconds, then the SYSTEM comes back to the player at irregular, story-shaped moments — a wire-service flash, a defector walk-in, a decrypt — each demanding a real choice. Your existing teletype engine is the delivery channel; espionage product should arrive as choice events, never as silent modifier changes.

findings.name: Twilight Struggle: covert ops abstracted to near-zero mechanics, yet it's the best Cold War espionage feel ever shipped
findings.detail: TS has no spies, no networks, no agencies — coups, destabilization, and influence ops are card plays with an Ops number, and the genius is the dual-use rule: playing an opponent-associated card for ops fires their event anyway, so nearly every action has a self-inflicted cost you chose eyes-open (gamesprecipice.com/twilightstruggle; theforge.defence.gov.au wargame-design analysis; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Struggle). Deniability/escalation is priced structurally: coups in battleground countries degrade DEFCON, and at DEFCON 2 a required coup can force you to trigger nuclear war and lose instantly — covert aggression literally spends escalation headroom. Hidden scoring cards mean each player acts on beliefs about what the opponent holds — 'what your rival believes' encoded in a hand of cards. Why it works: espionage isn't a subsystem, it's the OPPORTUNITY-COST STRUCTURE of the whole game — every covert act competes with everything else for the same scarce action, has a visible price, and touches the shared escalation meter. TS delivers maybe 7 decisions per turn and every one hurts.
findings.recommendation: This is the target texture for a 3-6-decisions-per-year game: covert action as a scarce, expensive play drawn from a shifting menu of opportunities (your event engine = the card deck), where the cost is always partly paid in the escalation/tension currency you've already built, and where acting reveals something about you (an op that fails or succeeds loudly moves rivals' beliefs about YOUR intent). Do not model tradecraft; price it.

findings.name: Invisible Inc & Phantom Doctrine: risk must be legible and clock-driven, not dice-driven
findings.detail: Invisible Inc's core device is the security-level clock: a visible counter rises every turn and on every detection, with new threats at FIXED, previewed increments — the player always knows what greed costs, so pushing for one more safe is an informed gamble, not a coin flip (gamedeveloper.com 'The Problems of Modern Stealth Design, and How Invisible Inc. Solves Them'). Phantom Doctrine went further and removed to-hit RNG entirely (shots resolve deterministically from Awareness and cover) and runs a hideout 'Danger' meter that only ever rises and can be managed but not reduced — you relocate before the raid (techraptor.net, gamespot.com reviews; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_Doctrine). Phantom Doctrine's commercial/critical failure was in mission repetition and teaching, not in these strategic devices — its Danger meter and no-RNG stance are the parts worth stealing. The shared principle: replace 'X% chance of catastrophe' rolls with an accumulating, visible EXPOSURE clock whose consequences trigger at known thresholds. This maps perfectly onto a deterministic sim: exposure accrual is reproducible, thresholds are explainable ('why did my network blow? — you ran three ops through it in 1951'), and player agency is preserved because they chose every increment.
findings.recommendation: Keep and promote your per-program exposure accumulator to the CENTER of the espionage design: every network and instrument carries a visible exposure value; every use adds a known amount; thresholds (rival counterintelligence tiers) are inspectable; blowback events fire deterministically from the accumulated total plus a seeded-RNG timing jitter. The player should always be able to answer 'how burned am I?' before acting.

findings.name: XCOM 2 covert actions: the good version of a mission menu — opportunity cost plus bounded, disclosed risk
findings.detail: WotC covert actions are non-combat menu picks: choose from a rotating slate, assign named soldiers, wait days, collect reward. What makes them respectable rather than fire-and-forget: (1) the cost is your best people being UNAVAILABLE — a genuine cross-layer opportunity cost against the tactical game; (2) each action discloses its specific risks up front (soldier wounded, ambush) and some risks can be bought off by adding a resource — risk is a line item, not a surprise; (3) the slate rotates, so it's a draft, not a tech tree — you pick 1 of N knowing the others expire; the designers explicitly cite CCG inspiration (steamcommunity.com WotC covert actions announcement; xcom.fandom.com/wiki/Covert_Actions; vigaroe.com XCOM 2 covert ops analysis). Residual criticism: rewards were sometimes so good the choice became obligatory rather than interesting — slate balance matters.
findings.recommendation: Present active operations as a small rotating slate (2-4 live opportunities, sourced from world state: a walk-in defector, a recruitable colonel, a purge creating disaffection) with disclosed risk line-items and a stated expiry. One slot, maybe two, for running ops at a time. Scarcity of slots plus expiring options generates your 3-6 real decisions per year without any per-agent micro.

findings.name: The tracking ceiling: Civ 6 and Terra Invicta show where agent-count micro dies
findings.detail: Civ 6 spies need reassignment every ~10 turns via a '3 click dance', and late-game counterspy coverage across many cities became a maintenance treadmill players begged to be able to turn off (steamcommunity.com/app/289070 'Most annoying feature : spies'). Terra Invicta's councilors — 4-6 named agents on a synchronized mission phase — are widely loved thematically yet drew a Steam thread literally titled 'Counselor micro is not fun': recurring chore missions (suppress xenoforming, purge spies, defend control points) turned characterful agents into a checklist (steamcommunity.com/app/1176470 discussions; pcgamer.com Terra Invicta review). Pattern across all cases: players comfortably track 3-6 espionage 'threads' when each thread is a STANDING POSTURE (this network watches Moscow) and choke when threads demand recurring per-cycle reassignment. Civ 5's veteran-spy death spiral (first successful spy snowballs, yours keeps dying to the rival's veteran) also shows per-agent XP creates rich-get-richer feedback that punishes the player RNG already hurt (forum.paradoxplaza.com 'Best and worst espionage experiences in games').
findings.recommendation: Hard cap simultaneous espionage entities at roughly 5: e.g., 3-4 standing country NETWORKS (postures, set-and-forget until an event) + 1-2 active operation slots. No per-cycle reassignment, ever. No agent XP ladders that compound wins.

findings.name: Named agents: charge them to the narrative budget, not the mechanics budget
findings.detail: Verdict from the evidence: named agents as MANAGED UNITS never earn their complexity in grand strategy — HoI4 operatives (recruit, place, upgrade, rescue) are the most-complained-about part of La Résistance; Terra Invicta's councilors, the best-realized named agents in the genre, still generated 'micro is not fun' threads; Civ's named spies are pure interchangeable pawns with a name painted on. Where names DO pay: as story texture at zero mechanical cost — XCOM covert actions borrow attachment from soldiers the player already knows; CK3's intrigue works because agents are characters who exist for other reasons. The Cold War fantasy specifically is about ASSETS and PRODUCT (VENONA, Penkovsky, Philby), not about leveling operatives — a mole should be a named, singular INSTRUMENT you hold and eventually burn, not a unit you move.
findings.recommendation: No recruitable/movable/level-up agent roster. Named individuals should appear only as event-borne singular assets: 'Colonel S., GRU, offers his services' arrives via teletype, becomes a card-like instrument with a codename, a product stream, and an exposure clock, and eventually dies, defects, or is burned — each transition a wire story. Names carry drama; the sim only tracks the instrument.

findings.name: Recommended core loop for UGS: two-layer 'coverage and cash-in' with event-shaped product
findings.detail: Synthesis of all precedents into an implementable shape. LAYER 1 — STANDING COLLECTION (the passive network, EU4-shaped, Stellaris-feedback-fixed): the player allocates a small fixed budget of collection capacity (stations/residencies) across target countries and picks a posture per target (Watch = safe, slow; Penetrate = builds assets, accrues exposure; Subvert = feeds the future ideology pillar). Coverage level per target is a single 0-100-ish number that directly drives estimate quality in systems you've ALREADY built: fuzz width on enemy military strength, bias on nuclear-program opacity estimates, and — the killer app — whether a planned economy's REPORTED output can be checked against ACTUAL. Low coverage doesn't just widen ranges; it lets the rival's deception (parades, inflated plan figures) pass unchallenged, which plugs espionage straight into the deterrence-from-beliefs machinery. Reallocating is rare and strategic (2-3 times a year at most), like moving an EU4 diplomat. LAYER 2 — OPERATIONS AND INSTRUMENTS (TS/XCOM-shaped): world events and coverage thresholds surface a rotating slate of 2-4 expiring opportunities via the teletype; the player holds 1-2 op slots. Ops are priced in money, coverage burn, EXPOSURE, and — for aggressive ones — tension/deniability, with risk line-items disclosed (Invisible Inc legibility) and resolution driven by exposure clocks plus forked SimRng, not naked percentage rolls. Successful collection ops yield INSTRUMENTS (a mole, a decrypt capability, kompromat) that persist and are cashed in at moments the PLAYER chooses — ideally inside crisis ladders, where 'I know their arsenal is half what they claim' is worth the most. Blowback is deterministic-from-exposure and arrives as wire stories (a U-2 shootdown analogue: caught assets spike tension and hand the rival a propaganda event), making deniability a real spendable currency. Cadence check: ~2 posture reallocations + ~3-4 slate picks/instrument cash-ins per year = 3-6 meaningful decisions, zero maintenance clicks, every number explainable ('your estimate narrowed because coverage in the USSR passed 60 and the Vienna residency turned a walk-in').
findings.recommendation: Build Layer 1 first — it monetizes three systems that already exist (fuzzed estimates, nuclear opacity, reported-vs-actual planned output) and needs only a coverage scalar per (player, target) pair wired into existing fuzz widths, replacing the hardcoded ones. Ship Layer 2 as teletype choice events with one op slot. Defer instruments/moles to a second pass once the slate loop proves out.

key_takeaways: Passive vs. active split is the right architecture, but every shipped grand-strategy version broke one side: EU4's active ops weren't worth the spend, HoI4's passive networks decayed into a maintenance chore, Stellaris's whole stack gave no feedback. The fix: passive coverage builds with zero upkeep and directly powers estimate quality; active ops are rare, expensive, and decisive.

The #1 chore generator is mandatory maintenance loops — HoI4's capture-rescue cycle and network decay, Civ 6's counterspy redeployment 'click dance', Terra Invicta's recurring councilor chores. Espionage decisions should be pull (opportunities arrive), never push (system demands upkeep).

Replace 'click op, wait 90 days, read popup' with intent-then-event cadence: orders take seconds, product returns as irregular teletype choice events (decrypt, walk-in, blown asset) that each demand a decision. UGS's existing wire/teletype engine is the natural delivery channel — Twilight Struggle's card deck, systematized.

Risk must be a legible clock, not a die roll: Invisible Inc's visible security level and Phantom Doctrine's monotonic Danger meter beat percentage-roll espionage everywhere they were tried. Promote UGS's exposure accumulator to the load-bearing mechanic: every use of a network adds known exposure; blowback fires at inspectable thresholds — perfectly compatible with the determinism contract.

Players track at most ~5 espionage threads, and only if they're standing postures rather than units. Cap the design at 3-4 country networks plus 1-2 operation slots; no agent roster, no per-agent XP (Civ 5's veteran-spy death spiral shows XP compounding punishes the loser twice).

Named agents don't earn unit-management complexity anywhere in the genre; they DO earn narrative weight as singular event-borne instruments (a codenamed mole with a product stream and an exposure clock, burned once, mourned on the wire).

The best espionage payoffs are held instruments and belief changes, not instant effects: CK3 hooks (leverage), TS's hidden hands, and — unique to UGS — narrowing fuzz ranges, piercing nuclear opacity bias, and exposing reported-vs-actual planned-economy divergence. Espionage should be the system that trades in the game's stated core currency: what your rival believes.

Aggressive covert action must spend escalation headroom, Twilight Struggle-style: coups and sabotage price into the global tension meter and deniability, so covert ops sit inside the brinkmanship pillar rather than beside it — and a blown op is a rival propaganda event, making deniability a real, losable currency.

reports.topic: The intelligence-quality economy: per-country 0-100 intel stat, collection sources 1950-1965, decay, counterintelligence, and how intel quality drives estimate width, estimate bias, deterrence, crisis resolve, and planned-economy transparency

findings.name: Core stat: three intel domains per (viewer, target) pair, stored as permille, displayed 0-100
findings.detail: HoI4's La Résistance splits intel into four 0-100% domains (army/navy/air/civilian) with hard reveal thresholds per decile — e.g. trade partners at 35% civilian, specific army techs at 70%, division template contents at 75% ([HoI4 wiki: Intel](https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Intel), [dev diary](https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/hoi4-dev-diary-intel.1295585/)). Four domains is too many for this game's few-meaningful-decisions sensibility, but ONE scalar is too few because the game's consumers are genuinely different: deterrence reads strategic-forces numbers, the Korean War slice reads order of battle, and the planned-economy reported-vs-actual gap is an economic secret that photography can never reveal. War in the East's per-unit Detection Level 0-10 ([WitE2 rules ch.10](https://dornshuld.chemistry.msstate.edu/rules/wite2/10-0.html)) shows the other pole — per-object granularity — which is too micro for grand strategy.
findings.recommendation: Store `IntelState { strategic: u32, military: u32, economic: u32 }` permille (0-1000) in a `BTreeMap<(CountryTag, CountryTag), IntelState>` resource (BTreeMap for determinism, per CLAUDE.md). Display each /10 as 0-100 in the dossier UI. Crisis-resolve estimates read a derived `political = (strategic + economic) / 2` rather than a fourth stored domain. Each collection source contributes to domains with fixed weights, so the player's real decision is source portfolio, not domain micromanagement. Update on `SimClock::new_month`, RNG via `rng.fork(b"intel")`.

findings.name: Growth model: each source grants a cap and a rate; intel asymptotically approaches the best cap (integer math)
findings.detail: HoI4 uses exactly this shape (sources raise a ceiling, passive decryption crawls toward it), and it is the right shape historically: embassies/attachés and FBIS open-source press analysis gave a permanent low baseline ([military attaché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_attach%C3%A9), [FBIS radio propaganda reports](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-PREX3-PURL-gpo49986/pdf/GOVPUB-PREX3-PURL-gpo49986.pdf)), while each better source class raised what was knowable, not how fast everything was learned. Asymptotic approach also gives diminishing returns for free.
findings.recommendation: Monthly, per domain: `cap = max over active sources of (source_cap * domain_weight / 1000)`, then if `intel < cap`: `intel += (cap - intel) * rate_permille / 1000 + 1` (the `+1` guarantees termination in integer math); rate_permille is the best active source's growth rate, 60-120 typical (reaches ~90% of cap in 2-3 game years at 100/1000 monthly). All constants in a `tuning` module, not literals.

findings.name: Source 1 — Embassy/attaché baseline: free, safe, capped low, tied to diplomatic relations
findings.detail: Attachés are declared intelligence officers; combined with open-source analysis (FBIS read Soviet press systematically, e.g. the June 1955 Literary Gazette analysis) this produced a real but shallow picture — order-of-magnitude force sizes, published figures, leadership. It costs nothing and risks nothing, which is why every state does it.
findings.recommendation: Automatic whenever diplomatic relations exist. Cap 250 permille all three domains, rate 150/month (fast to its low ceiling). Severed relations remove the source (see decay). This is the floor that makes intel 0-9 a rare state reserved for pariah pairs — at 0-24 the target's planned economy shows its REPORTED numbers verbatim with no 'figures suspect' flag, which is precisely the trap.

findings.name: Source 2 — Agent networks: the workhorse, priced in upkeep and risk, and the ONLY source for economic truth and resolve
findings.detail: HUMINT against the USSR was brutally hard: parachute infiltrations from ~1951 were routinely rolled up on landing, and by the mid-1950s the CIA had 'fewer than a dozen reliable penetrations' ([CIA activities in the Soviet Union](https://grokipedia.com/page/CIA_activities_in_the_Soviet_Union)). Yet a single asset — Penkovsky, 1961-62 — delivered IRBM installation footprints and the true weakness of the Soviet ICBM program, arguably deciding the Cuban crisis, before being caught and executed in 1963 ([Penkovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Penkovsky)). Networks are slow, cap-limited by the target's police state, and catastrophically lossy — but only humans read ledgers and intentions.
findings.recommendation: Built per target by command; setup cost + monthly upkeep (suggest 2 budget points/month at network size 1, scaling with size 1-3). Caps: economic 700, strategic 550, military 500 — reduced by `target_counterintel / 2` (the denied-area problem as a formula). Rate 60/month. Monthly roll-up roll (see counterintelligence finding). Add a rare 'walk-in defector' event (teletype choice event, weight scaled by target instability): accept for +150 economic/strategic intel decaying over 12 months, or refuse (he may be a plant — accepting when target counterintel ≥ 600 has a 250/1000 chance he is a dangle who injects +300 bias instead).

findings.name: Source 3 — SIGINT/decrypts: expensive standing program, reads the PAST, dies when ciphers change
findings.detail: Venona decrypted under 1% of intercepted Soviet cables over 37 years, ~3,000 messages total, with the bulk broken 1947-1952 — years after transmission — because one-time pads were reused ([NSA Venona history](https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/coldwar/venona_story.pdf), [Venona project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venona_project)). The Berlin tunnel (Operation Gold, 1955) cost $6.7M, intercepted ~500,000 calls — and was blown from day one by George Blake, with the Soviets protecting their mole by letting genuine traffic flow ([Operation Gold](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Operation_Gold)). Two lessons: SIGINT is retrospective and cheap per fact but fragile; and a compromised tap is the perfect bias-injection channel.
findings.recommendation: A standing agency investment (4 budget points/month) unlocking passive growth: caps military 450 / strategic 400 / economic 300, rate 50/month. Unique property: on activation, retroactively re-baselines the display fuzz seed so PAST months' shown estimates visibly 'correct themselves' in the wire archive — cheap to implement (the fuzz is already deterministic display-side) and dramatizes Venona. A 'cipher change' event (target-triggered when their counterintel crosses 600, or random ~1/36 monthly) zeroes the source for 6-18 months. Offer one Berlin-tunnel-style one-shot operation per target: large gain (+200 military intel over 6 months) but if target counterintel ≥ 700 it was blown from the start and instead injects +200 hidden bias — the player learns only from a later event.

findings.name: Source 4 — Overflights (1956+): mission commands, not passive collection; the bias-killer; shootdown risk that grows with target SAM tech
findings.detail: Eisenhower authorized U-2 overflights July 1956; ~24 deep penetrations were flown before May 1, 1960, when an SA-2 downed Powers on what was planned as the final flight — the Soviets had radar-tracked every mission but could not reach 70,000+ ft until the SA-2 matured ([State Dept](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1953-1960/u2-incident), [History.com](https://www.history.com/articles/u2-spy-incident)). Crucially, ONE photo — Saratov-Engels airfield, July 5, 1956, showing under three dozen Bisons against a claimed ~100 — killed the bomber gap ([Bomber gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomber_gap)). Photography is the verification source: it collapses systematic overestimation instantly, but only for countable hardware.
findings.recommendation: Tech-gated command (1956 historically). Per mission: 5 budget points, +60 strategic and +40 military intel (capped 850/750), AND sets a `verified_until = now + 24 months` timestamp that zeroes the deception/opacity bias term for strategic forces (see bias finding). Shootdown chance per mission: `target_sam_tech_level * 40` permille — ~0 in 1956, ~160 by 1960. On shootdown: +tension (major), teletype crisis event, overflights locked for 24 months (the historical 1960 gap that let the missile gap flourish), and the target gains a propaganda/deniability win. This makes each overflight a real decision with the exact historical texture: certainty purchased with escalation risk.

findings.name: Source 5 — Satellites (1960+): expensive, failure-prone at first, risk-free thereafter; ends strategic fog permanently but sees only hardware
findings.detail: Corona flew 12+ failures before Discoverer 14 succeeded on August 18, 1960, returning film covering 1.65M sq mi — more than ALL prior U-2 missions combined — at ~8m resolution, and promptly debunked the missile gap ([US Army on Corona](https://www.army.mil/article/173155/project_corona_americas_first_photo_reconnaissance_satellite), [Air & Space Forces](https://www.airandspaceforces.com/article/0995corona/)). No shootdown, no deniability cost, no pilot to parade in a courtroom. But film cannot see factory ledgers, morale, or intent.
findings.recommendation: Tech-gated program: 20 budget points to build + 3/month; first N launches have a failure chance decreasing 500→100 permille (rolled from `rng.fork(b"satellite")`), each failure a wire event. Once operational: automatic quarterly 'missions' at zero risk — caps strategic 900 / military 800 / economic 300, rate 120/month, and permanently maintains the `verified` flag for strategic forces. Deliberate design consequence: after ~1962 both superpowers' nuclear estimates converge toward truth, shifting the game's uncertainty onto the economic and political domains — which is exactly what happened, and keeps the late game about resolve and economics rather than counting.

findings.name: The two consumables: WIDTH shrinks with total intel, BIAS shrinks only with verification — wire this directly into the existing code
findings.detail: The codebase already separates these: `crates/ugs-app/src/war_ui.rs` (~line 52) applies hardcoded display fuzz widths; `crates/ugs-app/src/atomic_ui.rs` line 402 notes 'Historical NIEs overestimated: bias 1.0-2.6x'; `crates/ugs-sim/src/deterrence.rs` lines 181-212 computes `opacity = 1000 - exposure_permille`, `bias = 1000 + opacity * OPACITY_BIAS_PERMILLE / 1000 (+ DECEPTION_BIAS_PERMILLE)`. The bomber gap calibrates the ceiling: CIA projected 800 Bisons vs ~85 actual — but that extreme was CAUSED by the 1955 Aviation Day parade flying 10 Bisons in loops to simulate 60 ([Bomber gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomber_gap)); absent deception, overestimates ran nearer 1.5-2x. So max bias should decompose as baseline-opacity (~1.8x) + deception (~+0.8x) = 2.6x, matching the existing comment, and the parade toggle already exists (`deception: bool` in nuclear.rs line 165).
findings.recommendation: Width: `width_permille = 50 + (1000 - intel_domain) * 550 / 1000` — ±60% at intel 0, ±5% at 1000; replace war_ui's hardcoded fuzz widths with this, fed from the viewer's military intel. Bias (deterrence): replace `opacity = 1000 - exposure` with `knowledge = max(exposure_permille, viewer_strategic_intel)`, `opacity = 1000 - knowledge`; `bias = 1000 + opacity * 800 / 1000`; deception adds `+800 * (1000 - verification) / 1000` where `verification = 1000` while `verified_until` is current (overflight/satellite) else decays 50/month. Result: parade deception at low intel yields 2.6x (bomber gap), one overflight collapses it to ~1.0-1.1x (Saratov-Engels), and letting verification lapse lets bias regrow (the 1960-61 missile gap window). Keep exposure_permille as the floor — a leaky program is knowable even to a lazy rival; intel can only raise knowledge above it.

findings.name: Decile reveal table: what each intel tier buys, across all four pillars
findings.detail: HoI4's hard thresholds per decile are its best idea — players learn 'I need 70 to see techs' and collection becomes goal-directed ([HoI4 wiki: Intel](https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Intel)). Flashpoint Campaigns' contact-fidelity ladder (unknown contact → type → identified) is the same idea at tactical scale ([Flashpoint Campaigns](https://store.steampowered.com/app/330720/Flashpoint_Campaigns_Red_Storm_Players_Edition/)). Every threshold should be explainable in one clinical sentence in the dossier UI.
findings.recommendation: Displayed 0-100 (permille/10), per domain. 0-9: existence-level only; economy shows REPORTED figures verbatim, unflagged. 10-24 (embassy floor): total forces ±50-60%, published budgets, leadership dossiers, nuclear program existence unknown. 25-39: nuclear program EXISTS (yes/no), frontline unit locations, trade flows, width ±40%. 40-54: program stage (research/enrichment/assembled), 'figures suspect' flag on planned-economy output, width ±30%, deception ATTEMPTS detectable as an event ('attachés doubt flyby count'). 55-69: theater-level order of battle, warhead count band, estimated-ACTUAL economy band shown beside reported, width ±20%. 70-84: crisis resolve as a numeric band ±15, deliverable-vs-assembled distinction in deterrence panel, width ±12%. 85-100: width ±5%, bias ≤1.1x, actual economy output exact, and advance-warning wire events fire (mobilization, test preparations, crisis intentions). Below 70, resolve shows only qualitative words ('assessed: firm'); below 55, economy shows reported-only — the legibility cliff IS the incentive.

findings.name: Decay: sources lost means asymptotic decay toward the remaining floor; verification expires separately
findings.detail: Intelligence rots at different speeds: counted silos stay counted (the photo exists) but deployments, resolve, and economic figures go stale in months. The May 1960 overflight halt to August 1960 Corona success left exactly the window in which the missile gap myth peaked — decay is not flavor, it is a strategic window the target can exploit.
findings.recommendation: Monthly, per domain: `floor = max cap over still-active sources`; if `intel > floor`: `intel -= (intel - floor) * decay_permille / 1000 + 1`. decay_permille = 40 (half-life ~17 months) for military/economic, 25 for strategic (hardware ages slower). Verification is separate and harsher: `verified_until` lapses, then the bias term regrows at 50/month toward its opacity ceiling. Severed relations remove the embassy floor; a rolled-up network removes the agent source AND applies an immediate one-time `-150` to its domains (your best sub-sources were the ones arrested).

findings.name: Counterintelligence: one opposing 0-1000 stat funded from the same budget, three effects, and the double-agent bias weapon
findings.detail: The KGB's structural advantage was the closed society itself — informant networks and internal passports rolled up parachuted agents on landing ([CIA activities in the Soviet Union](https://grokipedia.com/page/CIA_activities_in_the_Soviet_Union)); and the best counterintelligence outcome was never the arrest but the turn: Blake let Moscow run the Berlin tunnel as a controlled channel for a year ([Operation Gold](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Operation_Gold)). Counterintel's crown jewel is making the enemy CONFIDENT and WRONG — which in this game's terms is bias injection, the mirror of the deception toggle, and directly serves 'what your rival believes matters as much as what is true'.
findings.recommendation: Per-country `counterintel: u32` permille = structural floor + funded component. Structural floor by regime type: authoritarian/closed 300, mixed 150, open 50 (the denied-area problem, and a real asymmetry: the USSR is hard to spy on but pays for it economically elsewhere). Funded: budget slider, ~3 points per +100, competing with collection funding — one agency budget, one allocation decision, no micro. Effects: (1) reduces rival agent-network caps by `counterintel / 2`; (2) monthly catch roll per hostile network: `chance = network_size * counterintel / 2000` permille from `rng.fork(b"ci-catch")` — on catch: wire event, +tension (minor, deniable — 'third secretary expelled'), rival loses the source and -150 intel; (3) at counterintel ≥ 600, a caught network is TURNED instead with 300/1000 chance: rival keeps their intel stat and their confidence (width stays narrow) but gains +300 hidden bias for 12 months — they are sure, and wrong, and only a verification source reveals it. Also gates cipher-change events against rival SIGINT at ≥ 600. Every effect surfaces to the VICTIM only probabilistically — you learn your network died, not always why.

key_takeaways: Three intel domains (strategic/military/economic) per (viewer,target) pair in permille, not HoI4's four and not one scalar: the game's existing consumers — deterrence, war-slice fuzz, planned-economy transparency — are genuinely different, and 'political' (crisis resolve) derives from the other domains rather than being stored.

Separate the two consumables: WIDTH (uncertainty band) shrinks with any intel; BIAS (systematic overestimation, already in deterrence.rs) shrinks only with verification-class sources (overflights 1956+, satellites 1960+). Calibrate to the bomber gap: baseline opacity bias ~1.8x plus parade deception ~+0.8x = 2.6x, matching the existing atomic_ui comment, collapsed by a single overflight as the Saratov-Engels photo did in July 1956.

Five sources with distinct shapes: embassy (free, cap 25), agent networks (upkeep + roll-up risk, sole access to economic truth and resolve — Penkovsky), SIGINT (standing cost, retroactive corrections, killed by cipher changes — Venona read <1%), overflights (per-mission commands buying certainty with shootdown/tension risk that grows with SAM tech), satellites (expensive, early failures, then risk-free permanent strategic verification — deliberately shifting late-game uncertainty onto economics and resolve).

Integer-math growth/decay: monthly `intel += (cap - intel) * rate/1000 + 1` toward the best active source cap; on source loss decay 25-40/1000 monthly toward the remaining floor; verification expires separately so bias regrows — reproducing the May-Aug 1960 window when the missile gap peaked.

Counterintelligence is one opposing stat with a regime-type structural floor (closed societies 300) plus funding from the SAME agency budget as collection — one allocation decision. Its best outcome is not the catch but the turn: at high CI a rolled network can be converted to a double-agent channel injecting hidden bias while the rival's confidence (narrow width) persists — deniable, believable, wrong.

Hard decile reveal thresholds (HoI4's best idea) make collection goal-directed and every shown number explainable: planned-economy REPORTED-only below 55, estimated-actual band 55-84, exact actual at 85+; crisis resolve qualitative below 70, numeric band above; each threshold one clinical dossier sentence.

Everything hangs on existing hooks: replace war_ui hardcoded fuzz widths with width(intel), replace deterrence opacity with max(exposure_permille, strategic_intel), keep exposure as the knowledge floor, reuse the deception bool as the bias source that verification cancels; BTreeMap storage, new_month cadence, rng.fork(b"intel") — all within the determinism contract.

reports.topic: Real intelligence work 1945-1962: institutions, operations, costs, failure rates, and must-have scripted events for a 1950-start Cold War grand strategy game

findings.name: Institutional scale and growth: intelligence agencies were tiny in 1950 and exploded during the Korean War
findings.detail: The CIA had roughly 5,000 employees worldwide in late January 1950; by 1953 it exceeded 10,000, with nearly 3,000 in the covert-action arm (OPC) and 3,000+ more overseas (CIA official history via encyclopedia.com; cia.gov Korean War retrospective). The Church Committee (Karalekas) figures are the canonical tuning curve: OPC went from 302 personnel and a $4.7M budget in 1949 to ~6,000 full-time and contract employees and $82M in 1952 — a ~17x budget increase in three years — and its overseas stations grew from 7 (1949) to 47 (by the early 1960s). By 1952 the merged clandestine directorate (DDP, formed 1 Aug 1952 from OPC+OSO) consumed three-quarters of the CIA budget and 60% of personnel (Wikipedia/OPC; spartacus-educational). On the Soviet side, the org chart churned with politics, not workload: NKGB renamed MGB March 1946 (chiefs: Merkulov to May 1946, Abakumov 1946-July 1951 — himself arrested in a purge — Ignatiev to Stalin's death 5 March 1953); MGB folded into Beria's MVD March 1953; Beria arrested June and shot December 1953; KGB created as a downgraded 'committee' 13 March 1954 under Ivan Serov (Britannica; Wikipedia MGB/KGB). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Policy_Coordination, https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/central-intelligence-agency, https://www.britannica.com/topic/KGB
findings.recommendation: Model the intelligence agency as a small, cheap institution in Jan 1950 that the player scales — capacity (stations, officers) should be buildable ~10-20x over 3-4 game years, gated by budget and by war-driven political will (a hot war should unlock a step-change in funding, mirroring NSC-68/Korea). Give the USSR a scripted 1953 succession disruption: Beria's fall should temporarily degrade Soviet intel effectiveness and offer defection windows (Petrov defected precisely because Beria's purge reached him). Covert-action capacity and espionage capacity should be separate tracks (OPC vs OSO) that the player can rebalance.

findings.name: Venona: the archetype of slow, silent, un-actionable-in-public intelligence
findings.detail: US Army signals program started 1943; Meredith Gardner broke into the second KGB codebook December 1946, reading a 1944 message listing Manhattan Project scientists; the bulk of exploitable messages were broken 1947-1952, all of WARTIME traffic — the product was years stale yet devastating. Venona identified 200+ covernames tied to KGB/GRU; Fuchs was identified from decrypts in summer 1949; Rosenberg covernames (ANTENNA/LIBERAL) surfaced 1947, FBI confirmed identity 1950. Critically, Venona was too secret to use in court — prosecutions needed confessions (Fuchs) or witnesses (Greenglass), and the USSR learned of it anyway via Weisband and Philby. Sources: https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/coldwar/venona_story.pdf, https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/venona/dyk.html
findings.recommendation: This is the strongest real-world validation of the game's belief-vs-truth pillar and deserves a mechanic: a long-running cryptanalysis program that yields RETROSPECTIVE intelligence (exposes moles/networks placed years earlier) rather than current-state info, and whose product cannot be publicly used — acting on it costs either a cover story (counterintel resource) or risks revealing the source. Scripted: a 'codebreak' event chain live at game start (US already reading 1944-45 traffic in Jan 1950) that periodically names a mole in the player's or ally's institutions.

findings.name: The mole problem: Cambridge Five and George Blake poisoned nearly every early Western operation
findings.detail: Philby was posted to Washington 1949-1951 as SIS liaison — sitting inside Venona and the Albania planning. Burgess and Maclean fled 25 May 1951, hours-to-days ahead of Maclean's scheduled interrogation (tipped by Philby); Philby was forced to resign from SIS July 1951 but was publicly exonerated in 1955 and only defected in January 1963 — twelve years of suspicion without proof (Hansard 7 Nov 1955; BBC). George Blake, SIS officer, betrayed the Berlin Tunnel to the KGB in late 1953/January 1954 — before construction began — and was only caught in 1961 via the Polish defector Goleniewski. Consequence pattern: the Albania drops were ambushed on arrival; the tunnel ran 11 months with the KGB knowing (they let it run to protect Blake); US-UK intelligence sharing was formally curtailed after Burgess/Maclean (newsletter.co.uk on UK-US security relations). Sources: https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/1955-11-07/debates/45728b3c-a5e0-48ac-829f-a47d00fec839/FormerForeignOfficeOfficials(Disappearance), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Gold, https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/uk-24803131
findings.recommendation: The mole should be the game's central counterintel object: a hidden modifier on YOUR side that silently converts your operations into the enemy's intelligence (raising their info quality and pre-blowing your covert ops) until found. Key design point from history: suspicion accumulates without proof — model a 'suspicion' state where the player can sideline a suspected officer (losing capacity) or keep them (risking continued leaks), and where a mole who flees (Burgess/Maclean event) causes a diplomatic/trust crisis with allies. Ally moles (a British Philby leaking American plans) let the player suffer leaks they cannot directly fix — a great source of ally friction.

findings.name: Great operations: costs, durations, and outcomes are well documented and surprisingly cheap
findings.detail: Berlin Tunnel (Operation Gold/Stopwatch): planned from 1953, dug 1954-Feb 1955, taps live ~11 May 1955 to 22 April 1956 (11 months 11 days), cost $6.5-6.7M; yield 50,000 reels of tape, 443,000 transcribed conversations, 1,750 reports — and it was blown before ground was broken, though most historians judge the take largely genuine because the KGB protected Blake rather than feed disinformation (Wikipedia Operation Gold; Vogel, Betrayal in Berlin). Iran TPAJAX: planning from ~March 1953, $1M released to Tehran station April 1953, coup succeeded 19 August 1953 — roughly a 5-month operation, and it nearly failed on 15-16 August before succeeding on the second attempt (FRUS 1951-54 Iran; history.stanford.edu). Guatemala PBSUCCESS: authorized August 1953, executed 18-27 June 1954 — ~10 months, $2.7M budget, 480-man proxy force plus psywar radio and a few aircraft (militarystrategymagazine.com; FRUS 1952-54 Guatemala). Italy 1948: at least $1M direct CIA spend (estimates $10-20M total effort), then ~$5M/year sustained political subsidies into the 1960s (National Security Archive). U-2: $22.5M Lockheed contract Dec 1954, first flight Aug 1955, first Soviet overflight 4 July 1956, ~24 deep overflights total until Powers shot down 1 May 1960 — which collapsed the Paris summit 16 May 1960 after Khrushchev caught Eisenhower in a public lie (NASA/Britannica; history.state.gov). Corona: ~12 straight failures 1959-mid-1960, first capsule recovery (Discoverer 13) 11 Aug 1960, and Discoverer 14 (18 Aug 1960) returned more USSR photo coverage than ALL U-2 flights combined. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Gold, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1951-54Iran/ch3, https://www.militarystrategymagazine.com/article/operation-pbsuccess-u-s-covert-action-in-guatemala/, https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/intelligence/2017-02-07/cia-covert-aid-italy-averaged-5-million-annually-late-1940s, https://history.state.gov/milestones/1953-1960/u2-incident, https://www.airandspaceforces.com/article/0995corona/
findings.recommendation: Tuning anchors: a regime-change covert action costs $1-3M and takes 5-10 months; an election intervention costs ~$1M per cycle plus ~$5M/yr maintenance; a major technical collection coup (tunnel) costs ~$7M and ~2 years planning-to-blown; a strategic reconnaissance program costs $20-100M+ and 1-2 years R&D with a catastrophic-exposure tail risk. In 1950 dollars these are trivial next to military budgets ($13B+ US defense pre-Korea) — the game should make covert ops CHEAP in money but expensive in deniability, tension, and blowback, which matches both history and the vision doc. The U-2 arc (huge intel gain, then one shootdown wrecks a summit and hands the rival a propaganda win) is the perfect template for a high-risk collection asset the player must decide when to STOP using; Corona should then obsolete it — reward for tech patience through visible failures.

findings.name: Failure rates: agent infiltration into denied areas was a near-total loss, and the enemy played the networks back
findings.detail: Albania (Operation Valuable/BGFIEND, 1949-1954): CIA's FIEND phase inserted 83 agents by sea/air, 37 confirmed killed or captured (~45% confirmed loss; effective mission success ~0); combined UK/US operation losses including local recruits and reprisals run 300-961 killed/captured depending on counting (Wikipedia Operation Valuable; CIA Reading Room BGFIEND files). Ukraine (early AERODYNAMIC, 1949-1953): 12 agents airdropped, ALL but one captured or killed (Intelligence & National Security, 'All the heroes are dead', 2024). China Third Force: agent team in Manchuria was captured and DOUBLED; the pickup flight was ambushed November 1952 — Downey (life sentence) and Fecteau (20 years) imprisoned, sentences announced 1954; the CIA denied their affiliation until 1973 (CIA Studies in Intelligence, 'Two CIA Prisoners in China'). Root causes recur: moles (Philby sat on the Albania liaison committee), doubled radio operators, and police-state environments where strangers cannot survive. Notably the KGB/Sigurimi preferred to play networks back (funkspiel) rather than announce arrests — the sponsor believed dead networks were alive for months or years. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Valuable, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/02684527.2024.2422136, https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Two-CIA-Prisoners-China.pdf
findings.recommendation: Give paramilitary infiltration of hardened police states a brutal base failure rate (80-95% network roll-up within 6-18 months) that the PLAYER'S INTELLIGENCE DOES NOT REPORT HONESTLY: a rolled-up network should keep transmitting (enemy-controlled) and keep consuming budget, showing fake product, until a counterintel check or defector reveals it. This is the intel pillar's version of the economy pillar's reported-vs-actual divergence and should reuse that pattern. A captured officer (Downey/Fecteau event) creates a years-long deniability liability: admit and pay tension, or deny and forfeit the man. Success odds should scale with target openness — denied-area ops fail; ops in contested/open countries (Iran, Guatemala, Italy) succeed cheaply — giving players a legible strategic geography of where covert action works.

findings.name: Defectors and spy trials were the era's public shocks — they moved domestic politics and international tension on specific dates
findings.detail: Gouzenko (GRU cipher clerk, Ottawa, defected 5 September 1945 with 109 documents) exposed atomic espionage networks in Canada, triggered the Feb 1946 Kellock-Taschereau Royal Commission and Nunn May's arrest, and is conventionally dated as the Western public's Cold War wake-up. Fuchs: confessed 24 January 1950, tried at the Old Bailey 1 March 1950 — the whole trial under two hours — 14-year maximum sentence (USSR was not legally an enemy); his confession led directly to Gold, Greenglass, and the Rosenbergs (Julius arrested 17 July 1950, Ethel 11 August 1950; tried March 1951; executed 19 June 1953, the only US civilian executions for Cold War espionage), and fed Truman's 31 Jan 1950 H-bomb decision context (history.blog.gov.uk; famous-trials.com). McCarthy's Wheeling speech came 9 February 1950 — sixteen days after Fuchs confessed. Petrov (MVD resident, Canberra) defected 3 April 1954 amid the post-Beria purge; his wife's dramatic tarmac rescue 19-20 April and the Royal Commission (from 3 May 1954) broke off Soviet-Australian diplomatic relations until 1959 and detonated Australian domestic politics (the Labor split). Sources: https://history.blog.gov.uk/2020/03/02/whats-the-context-sentencing-of-atomic-spy-klaus-fuchs-1-march-1950, https://famous-trials.com/rosenberg/2003-fuchs, https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/1955-11-07/debates/45728b3c-a5e0-48ac-829f-a47d00fec839/FormerForeignOfficeOfficials(Disappearance)
findings.recommendation: Spy trials and defections are the natural bridge between the intel pillar and the tension meter/teletype engine you already have: a caught foreign spy is a CHOICE event — quiet trade/turn (intel value, no tension), public trial (domestic cohesion up, global tension up, rival embarrassed, but your own paranoia/purge pressure rises), or execution (max tension, hardens rival). Defectors should be the primary mechanism by which fuzzed estimates SNAP to truth: a walk-in delivers a one-time large reduction in uncertainty about the rival (and exposes moles), with incidence spiking during the rival's internal purges. The Fuchs-to-McCarthy sequence argues for a domestic 'spy scare' track where public exposures compound into loyalty purges that damage your OWN institutions — historical US mirror of the Soviet purge mechanic.

findings.name: Must-have scripted events for a 1950 start, in order
findings.detail: Already-in-motion at game start: Venona readouts (ongoing), Fuchs confession/trial (24 Jan / 1 Mar 1950), McCarthy's Wheeling speech (9 Feb 1950), Rosenberg arrests (Jul-Aug 1950). Then: CIA's Korea surprise failures (invasion 25 June 1950 and Chinese intervention Oct-Nov 1950 — both intelligence-failure post-mortems, cia.gov Korean War retrospective); Albania/Ukraine drop disasters (1949-1953, rolling); Burgess-Maclean flight (25 May 1951) with Philby suspicion aftermath; Rosenberg execution (19 June 1953) as a tension/protest event; Beria's fall (June-Dec 1953) opening the defection window; Petrov defection (3 April 1954); TPAJAX (Aug 1953) and PBSUCCESS (June 1954) as player-drivable covert-action templates rather than fixed events; Berlin Tunnel window (1954-April 1956, its value inverted if the rival has a mole); U-2 era (1956-1960) ending in a Powers-style shootdown risk event that can wreck an ongoing summit; Corona payoff (Aug 1960) that collapses estimate uncertainty and — historically — DEFLATED the missile-gap belief, i.e., truth arriving can REDUCE tension. Pre-1950 backstory (Gouzenko 1945, Italy 1948) belongs in starting-state flavor: the West starts already alarmed, Italy starts already bought.
findings.recommendation: Script the fixed-date public shocks (Fuchs, Burgess/Maclean, Rosenberg execution, Petrov, Beria) as teletype/choice events with tension and estimate-accuracy effects; implement the operations (Ajax-style coup, tunnel-style tap, U-2-style overflight program, Corona-style satellite) as generic player-initiated systems with the historical instances as the AI/default flavoring. The single most game-shaped historical loop to build first: overflight/collection asset -> better estimates -> deterrence recalculation -> exposure risk event -> summit/tension consequences, because it wires the new intel pillar directly into the already-implemented deterrence-from-biased-estimates machinery.

key_takeaways: Covert action was astonishingly cheap in money ($1-3M for a coup, $6.7M for the Berlin Tunnel, ~$1M for the 1948 Italian election) but expensive in deniability and blowback — price ops in political currency, not cash, and let cash be almost trivial next to military budgets.

Agent infiltration into police states failed at 80-95%+ (Albania: 37+ of 83 CIA agents lost; Ukraine: 11 of 12; China: team doubled, officers imprisoned 20 years) and the enemy played dead networks back — model rolled-up networks that keep reporting fake product, mirroring the economy pillar's reported-vs-actual divergence.

Moles were the dominant failure cause (Philby blew Albania and Venona awareness; Blake blew the tunnel pre-construction) and suspicion lingered for years without proof — a hidden your-side mole with a slow suspicion mechanic is the core counterintel game object.

Intelligence product arrives stale, secret, and unusable in public (Venona read 1944 traffic in 1948-52 and couldn't be cited in court): separate 'knowing' from 'being able to act openly on it'; acting risks the source.

Institutions scale fast under war pressure: OPC went 302 staff/$4.7M (1949) to ~6,000/$82M (1952); the Korean War doubled the CIA — make hot war the step-change unlock for intel capacity, and script Soviet purge cycles (Abakumov 1951, Beria 1953) as defection windows and effectiveness dips.

Public spy shocks moved history on precise dates (Fuchs 1 Mar 1950 -> McCarthy 9 Feb 1950 sixteen days after the confession; Burgess/Maclean 25 May 1951; Rosenberg execution 19 Jun 1953; Petrov 3 Apr 1954; Powers 1 May 1960 killing the Paris summit 16 May) — these are ready-made teletype choice events tied to the tension meter.

Technical collection follows an arc the game should reproduce: high-risk manned overflight (U-2, 1956-60) yields great estimates until one shootdown detonates a crisis; satellites (Corona, Aug 1960, more coverage than every U-2 flight combined) then obsolete it — and truth arriving can LOWER tension, as Corona deflated the missile gap.

reports.topic: Covert operations design: honest risk presentation, blowback, deniability mechanics, op lifecycle, and a 1950s operation catalog

findings.name: Show outcome branches, not success percentages (Invisible Inc / Into the Breach doctrine)
findings.detail: Invisible Inc's core insight is that giving the player 'perfect, reliable, hard-and-fast intel' about consequences turns stealth from guesswork into strategy (Game Developer: 'The Problems of Modern Stealth Design', gamedeveloper.com; Tom Francis, pentadact.com). Into the Breach telegraphs every enemy action so 'every death felt like your own fault' — the player sees exactly which tile gets hit and what breaks (GDC 2019 Design Postmortem, gdcvault.com/play/1025772). Meanwhile XCOM's percentage popup is the genre's most famous failure of risk communication: the '95% miss' meme shows that a bare probability reads as betrayal, not information, and Firaxis had to secretly inflate odds to compensate (Steam forums; gameplayask.blog on hidden hit-chance modifiers). This matches the project's prior Unity-of-Command finding that concrete forecasts beat odds ratios.
findings.recommendation: Never show 'Success chance: 62%'. Before commitment, show the full OUTCOME LADDER as concrete world-states: e.g. for an overflight — 'CLEAN: photographic coverage of 3 suspected sites / DETECTED: diplomatic protest, tension +minor, no evidence / SHOOTDOWN: pilot status unknown, evidence in enemy hands, deniability at risk'. Attach qualitative likelihood words drawn from real intelligence-estimate language (ALMOST CERTAIN / PROBABLE / POSSIBLE / UNLIKELY) computed deterministically from visible factors the player can inspect — this also satisfies the 'every number explainable' pillar. The player gambles on WHICH branch, never on whether the UI lied.

findings.name: Failure must be theater, not a penalty number — the U-2 arc is the archetype
findings.detail: The U-2/Powers incident is a complete dramatic structure: shootdown (May 1 1960) → US issues pre-planned NASA 'weather plane' cover story → Khrushchev springs the trap on May 7 by revealing the pilot is alive and has confessed → Eisenhower caught in a public lie → Paris four-power summit collapses when Khrushchev storms out (Eisenhower Library, eisenhowerlibrary.gov; history.state.gov/milestones/1953-1960/u2-incident; history.com). The critical design detail: the cover story itself became the disaster. The lie, once disproven by a live pilot, cost more than the espionage. Blowback likewise historically runs through captured personnel: AP correspondent William Oatis got a scripted show trial in Prague in 1951 with a coerced confession, 120 ticketed spectators, and a 10-year sentence, released only after Stalin died (Radio Prague, radio.cz; Nieman Reports); businessman Robert Vogeler served 17 months in Hungary after a 1950 espionage show trial (researchgate.net ITT/Vogeler paper).
findings.recommendation: A failed op should spawn a multi-week EVENT ARC, not a stat hit: (1) initial wire flash with facts unclear; (2) a cover-story choice event — deny everything / limited hangout / acknowledge — chosen BEFORE the player knows what evidence the enemy holds (Powers' survival was unknown when the NASA story ran); (3) enemy reveal, timed for maximum damage — the AI should hold evidence to detonate before summits and conferences; (4) downstream consequences: show trial of captured agents (propaganda ticks for the enemy, periodic wire coverage), prisoner-exchange bargaining chip, summit/negotiation collapse, tension spike scaled by how loudly the cover story was disproven. Denying-then-being-proven-wrong must cost strictly more than admitting early — that's the U-2 lesson and it makes the cover-story choice a real decision.

findings.name: Deniability as a degrading currency with three attribution states
findings.detail: NSC 10/2 (June 1948) defines covert operations as those 'so planned and executed that... if uncovered the US Government can plausibly disclaim any responsibility' (irp.fas.org/eprint/berger.htm; Wikipedia: Plausible deniability). Cormac & Aldrich's 'Grey is the new black' (International Affairs 94:3, academic.oup.com) adds the crucial nuance: deniability was 'deeply problematic even in its supposed heyday'; many operations were open secrets, yet states kept the fiction going because IMPLAUSIBLE deniability still has value — unacknowledged interference creates ambiguity that constrains the victim's response even when everyone 'knows'. This maps perfectly onto the game's existing belief-vs-truth architecture and the military slice's deniability-as-strippable-currency for volunteer formations.
findings.recommendation: Give every op an attribution state visible to both sides: UNATTRIBUTED → SUSPECTED (enemy believes with some confidence, can protest but pays a credibility cost if wrong) → PROVEN (physical evidence: captured agent, aircraft wreckage, documents, a public confession). Evidence is generated by outcome branches, discrete and named ('pilot in custody', 'radio transmitter recovered'), not an abstract meter — the player can see exactly which objects hang over them. SUSPECTED ops let the victim retaliate covertly or spend tension to protest; only PROVEN ops work as public crisis pretexts, justify formal sanctions/ultimatums, and strip the sponsor's standing deniability discount on volunteer formations. Key rule from Cormac & Aldrich: even PROVEN ops that were never officially acknowledged cost less than acknowledged ones — the fiction itself dampens escalation, which is why both superpowers maintained it. That's a mechanical reason the failure state (total war) stays avoidable.

findings.name: Ongoing ops accumulate breaches; discovery is the enemy letting you run (CK3 + Berlin Tunnel)
findings.detail: CK3's scheme system is the best long-running-op model in strategy games: hostile schemes have a Secrecy value, failed secrecy causes discrete Breaches (agent exposed, existence leaked), success chance drops per breach, five breaches auto-fail (CK3 Dev Diary #5, forum.paradoxplaza.com). The Berlin Tunnel (Operation Gold/REGAL) adds the darker historical wrinkle: the KGB knew about the tunnel from inception via mole George Blake, let it run 11 months to protect him, then staged an 'accidental discovery' in April 1956 (cia.gov/legacy/museum Berlin Tunnel exhibit; NSA Operation REGAL history, nsa.gov). Similarly the entire Albania operation was blown from the start by Kim Philby, and nearly every inserted team met 'capture, interrogation, show trial, or execution' (Wikipedia: Operation Valuable; Foreign Policy review of 'A Rich Harvest of Bitter Fruit', foreignpolicy.com).
findings.recommendation: Long-running ops (networks, taps, radios) should tick a visible per-op EXPOSURE track fed by discrete, explainable breach events ('courier detained in Vienna', 'transmitter triangulated') — extending the existing per-program exposure accumulator to ops. Twist worth building: when the AI discovers a network, it should sometimes choose to WATCH rather than roll it up — feeding the player subtly corrupted intelligence (which plugs directly into the existing biased-estimate machinery) or timing the public roll-up for a diplomatic moment. The player can burn an op preemptively (safe, sunk cost) or ride a high-exposure op for more product — the Berlin Tunnel dilemma. Late-game counterintelligence can reveal 'this op was blown as of [date]', retroactively poisoning intelligence the player already acted on.

findings.name: Op lifecycle: five phases, three player decisions, the rest resolves automatically
findings.detail: Terra Invicta is the cautionary tale for over-decisioning: every councilor rolls contested missions every phase, producing constant low-stakes percentage rolls and detection checks (Terra Invicta wiki, hoodedhorse.com; Pavonis Dev Diary #8). The project's design sensibility (few meaningful decisions, no micro) demands the opposite: XCOM's strategic layer works because you choose the mission and loadout, then the mission resolves as drama, not paperwork. Historical ops had exactly this shape — Ajax and PBSuccess were months of preparation, authorization at the top (Eisenhower/NSC), then execution largely out of Washington's hands (history.state.gov FRUS Guatemala compilation; Wikipedia: 1953 Iranian coup).
findings.recommendation: Lifecycle: (1) AUTHORIZE — player picks op type, target, and a posture dial (cautious/standard/aggressive: trades prep time and cost against outcome-ladder odds and evidence-if-blown; aggressive ops leave more evidence). This is the big decision, presented with the full outcome ladder. (2) PREPARATION — weeks/months of sim time; exposure can breach during prep; player may abort cleanly (real ops died in prep constantly). (3) EXECUTION — resolves automatically over hours/days via SimRng fork; NO mid-op micro. (4) OUTCOME REVEAL — arrives as a wire report, possibly delayed or initially wrong (the player's own damage assessment should itself be an estimate: 'results of the Tirana insertion remain unconfirmed'). (5) ATTRIBUTION AFTERMATH — the only other decision point: cover-story stance, disavow-or-trade captured agents, exploit-or-bank evidence you've captured about THEIR ops. Three decisions per op, each meaningful; everything else is deterministic sim.

findings.name: Clinical teletype voice: ops read as wire copy and damage assessments, never as game-speak
findings.detail: The game already has a teletype/wire engine and a bureaucratic period voice. The historical registers to steal from: wire-service flashes (the U-2 story broke via NASA's actual press release about a 'weather research aircraft' missing north of Turkey — nps.gov/articles/000/u-2-incident.htm), intelligence-estimate hedging language, and the deliciously self-defeating clandestine-radio style of PBSuccess's 'Voice of Liberation': 'It is not true that the waters of Lake Atitlan have been poisoned' and 'we are unable to confirm or deny that Castillo Armas has an army of 5,000 men' (militarystrategymagazine.com on PBSUCCESS; allthatsinteresting.com).
findings.recommendation: Three distinct textual registers, all deadpan: (1) PUBLIC WIRE — what the world sees, in period wire style ('PRAGUE (AP) — AN AMERICAN CITIZEN WAS DETAINED TUESDAY...'), identical for both sides' ops; the player reads their own blown op as a news item like everyone else. (2) INTERNAL CABLE — the player's own channel: numbered paragraphs, estimate language ('1. TEAM CHARLIE INSERTED 0300 LOCAL. 2. NO CONTACT SINCE. ASSESS CAPTURE PROBABLE.'), damage assessments that are themselves fuzzy. (3) ENEMY BROADCAST — TASS/Radio Moscow communiqués and show-trial coverage when your op is blown, dripping over weeks. Never show a 'Mission Failed -15 Deniability' toast; the wire copy IS the outcome reveal, and hovering any consequence decomposes it into the explainable numbers underneath.

findings.name: Operation type 1 — Aerial reconnaissance overflight (the intelligence-for-risk trade)
findings.detail: Pre-U-2, the US flew RB-45/RB-47 penetration flights and Genetrix camera balloons; the U-2 program (1956-60) traded extraordinary intelligence on Soviet capabilities against escalating shootdown risk as SAM technology improved, ending exactly as feared on May 1 1960 (eisenhowerlibrary.gov; britannica.com/event/U-2-Incident). This is THE bridge op to the nuclear pillar: overflights are how you narrow the opacity bias on enemy program estimates.
findings.recommendation: Decision: route depth (border ferret / shallow / deep penetration) over chosen intel targets. Payoff: directly shrinks the error bars and opacity bias on enemy nuclear-program and military-strength estimates — the mechanical connective tissue to systems already built. Risk model: shootdown likelihood grows with depth, repetition over the same corridors, and enemy air-defense tech level (a visible, dated capability the player can track — 'assess SA-2 coverage of route as of March 1958'). Failure theater: wreckage + pilot-status-unknown window → cover story choice → possible live-pilot reveal → trial, tension spike, summit damage. Clean failure branch exists too: mechanical abort, no evidence.

findings.name: Operation type 2 — Émigré network insertion (slow build, catastrophic downside)
findings.detail: Operation Valuable/Fiend (1949-54): CIA/MI6 inserted émigré teams into Albania by sea and parachute to foment rebellion; Philby's betrayal meant nearly every team was captured, tried, or executed, and the operation is the canonical 'dismal failure' of early covert action (Wikipedia: Operation Valuable; foreignpolicy.com review). Captured agents fed enemy show trials and radio-game deceptions (the Soviets played back captured radios to lure more teams).
findings.recommendation: Decision: target country + network purpose (intelligence / sabotage-capable / insurrection seed — each later op type needs the matching network as a prerequisite, making this the infrastructure op). Long prep, cheap upkeep, per-network exposure track. Failure theater is the richest in the game: captured teams enable enemy RADIO PLAYBACK — the network shows as alive but feeds fabricated intelligence into your estimate machinery until counterintelligence catches it; then show trials and executions as recurring wire items naming the agents (the division-naming tech already built should extend to named agents with homes and graves). Networks in a country also silently die if that country's security services get funded/purged — creating cross-pillar interactions.

findings.name: Operation type 3 — Coup sponsorship (the campaign op: Ajax/PBSuccess)
findings.detail: Ajax (Iran 1953) established the template — bribing officials, planting press stories, organized mobs, suborning military officers (Wikipedia: 1953 Iranian coup; mises.org analysis); PBSuccess (Guatemala 1954) added the psywar layer: Voice of Liberation radio presenting a tiny invasion force as unstoppable, so the Guatemalan army refused to fight and Árbenz resigned — victory by manufactured belief, not force (militarystrategymagazine.com; adst.org oral histories). Both required months of preparation and multiple sub-operations, and both were 'open secrets' regionally — deniability was thin from day one (Cormac & Aldrich).
findings.recommendation: Make this the CAPSTONE op, not a button: it requires prerequisites (a network in-country, a funded opposition figure, ideally a clandestine radio) and runs as a staged campaign where each stage emits wire copy and can abort. Success chance should be dominated by the TARGET GOVERNMENT'S BELIEVED strength versus its actual cohesion — the PBSuccess mechanism: your radio op inflates the perceived rebel strength, and the government's will breaks against the perception. This literally reuses the game's belief-vs-truth machinery as the win condition of the op. Failure theater: a failed coup is a PROVEN-attribution disaster — dead assets, a hostile government now aligned with your rival, a propaganda gift, and (per Guatemala's aftermath) a regional legitimacy cost that boosts rival influence on the whole continent.

findings.name: Operation types 4-5 — Influence ops: clandestine radio and balloon leaflets (low-risk, low-deniability-cost volume plays)
findings.detail: Free Europe Press launched 590,415 balloons carrying ~301 million leaflets into Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland 1951-56 (Operations Prospero 1953, Veto 1954, Focus 1954-55, Spotlight 1955), including translations of Animal Farm; Czechoslovakia responded with MiGs and AA guns shooting at balloons and formal diplomatic protests (rferl.org; coldwarradiomuseum.com; Centaurus journal, onlinelibrary.wiley.com). These ops were barely deniable and nobody cared — they were cheap, continuous, and the enemy's overreaction was itself a propaganda win.
findings.recommendation: Model radio/leaflet ops as toggled STANDING PROGRAMS, not discrete ops: ongoing budget, continuous small influence/unrest drip into target provinces, near-zero agent risk, SUSPECTED-forever attribution that never reaches PROVEN (a balloon is not a pilot). Their real design role: they give the ideology pillar its cheapest lever, they seed the unrest preconditions that insurrection-type ops need, and enemy counter-reactions (shooting at balloons, jamming) generate wire flavor and tiny tension ticks. Include the enemy jamming response as a visible budget the rival must pay — asymmetric cost imposition.

findings.name: Operation types 6-7 — SIGINT cable tap and defector inducement/exfiltration (product ops)
findings.detail: The Berlin Tunnel yielded 'reams of material about Soviet military capabilities, operations, and plans' for 11 months at enormous cost, while being compromised the entire time (cia.gov Berlin Tunnel exhibit; warfarehistorynetwork.com). Defectors were the other great product source — and the KGB's answering op was abduction: Walter Linse kidnapped from West Berlin in July 1952 and executed; dozens of Berlin/Vienna abductions in the early 50s (berndpulch.org KGB/Stasi study; theins.org on KGB retribution operations).
findings.recommendation: CABLE TAP: expensive one-time dig at a named location, then a standing intelligence feed that reduces estimate bias across a whole category (enemy military dispositions, not just one program) — strictly better product than overflights but immobile and mole-vulnerable; discovery is quiet (feed degrades or turns poisoned) rather than loud, making it the paranoia op. DEFECTOR INDUCEMENT: targeted at named enemy program scientists/officers (uranium and nuclear-program staff already exist as data); success delivers a one-time deep-truth snapshot of one enemy program (temporarily zeroing its opacity bias) plus a propaganda wire event; failure means the candidate was a dangle — planted disinformation enters your estimates. The Soviet mirror op is ABDUCTION of your defectors/émigré leaders: recovers their secrets, intimidates diaspora networks, but at SUSPECTED attribution and a small taboo cost.

findings.name: Operation type 8 — Executive action (assassination/abduction): the taboo-priced op
findings.detail: Stashinsky's poison-spray assassinations of Ukrainian émigrés Rebet (1957) and Bandera (1959) were ordered from the top — approved by KGB chairman Shelepin and Khrushchev — and when Stashinsky defected in 1961 his Karlsruhe trial became 'the most publicized assassination case in Cold War history', pinning state murder on Moscow before the world (spotterup.com; theins.org). The blowback wasn't tension — it was PROVEN attribution of the most norm-violating op class, delivered by a defecting perpetrator years later.
findings.recommendation: Include it precisely because the game has a taboo system: executive action against named émigré leaders/defectors/coup figures should be the cheapest way to remove a problem and the most expensive when proven — echoing the nuclear-taboo architecture with a lesser 'assassination norm'. Distinctive risk model: the evidence is a PERSON (the operator), and the attribution event can fire YEARS later when that operator defects — a delayed fuse the player cannot see ticking, priced into the outcome ladder as 'PROVEN ATTRIBUTION: POSSIBLE, TIMING UNKNOWABLE'. This is the one op where the honest forecast is honest about its own unknowability, which is itself a deterrent to using it — correct for both realism and the total-war-avoidance thesis.

findings.name: Operation types 9-10 — Party/election bankrolling and deniable arms pipelines (the currency ops)
findings.detail: Funding friendly parties, unions, and front organizations was the bread-and-butter covert action of both sides — the CIA's Italian election intervention model, Moscow's international front organizations and party subsidies (berger analysis at irp.fas.org; Cormac & Aldrich on routine unacknowledged interference). Arms pipelines to proxies were the standing military variant, connecting directly to the volunteer-formation deniability flag already implemented in the Korean War slice.
findings.recommendation: PARTY FUNDING: recurring budget line into a named country's aligned party/unions, shifting the (future) alignment drift; exposure event ('financing scandal') embarrasses the local party more than the sponsor — the blowback lands on the asset, a distinct and interesting shape. ARMS PIPELINE: enables/strengthens volunteer formations and insurgents while setting their deniability level; interdiction events (a captured shipment with factory markings) are the evidence objects that degrade attribution state for the WHOLE proxy relationship, unifying the espionage layer with the already-built military deniability currency. Both are standing programs: they give the covert layer its economy — a finite covert budget forced across standing programs vs discrete ops is the macro decision that keeps op count low.

findings.name: The defender's side: counterintelligence and the show trial as an operation
findings.detail: Every blown Western op became enemy content: Oatis's trial was 'orchestrated down to the smallest detail' with a coerced confession and ticketed audience (radio.cz); Albania's captured teams were tried publicly; Powers's Moscow trial was a global media event. The Eastern bloc treated the SHOW TRIAL itself as a covert-action product — manufacturing proof, sometimes from innocents (Oatis was a journalist, not a spy — theconversation.com), because a confession on the record moved world belief regardless of truth.
findings.recommendation: Give the defender verbs, or the covert layer is solitaire: a COUNTERINTELLIGENCE SWEEP standing program (raises breach rates on foreign ops in your territory, costs budget and — for the open society — a small domestic-legitimacy or economy cost, a real 1950s tradeoff); and a SHOW TRIAL discrete op usable on any captured foreigner, which converts a prisoner into propaganda + a fabricated PROVEN-attribution claim that the accused sponsor must respond to even when innocent (the Oatis case).
